notes.b: The appendicular skeleton is the skeleton of the limbs and of the two girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton (the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum). It is the part of the skeleton that lets you reach, walk and run.
points: A girdle is a ring or half-ring of bones that anchors a pair of limbs to the trunk. The pectoral (shoulder) girdle attaches the arms, and the pelvic (hip) girdle attaches the legs.

Its main job is movement, because the limb bones act as levers for the muscles that pull on them. The legs and pelvic girdle also bear the body's weight, so they are built for strength as well as movement.
notes.tip: The clavicle and scapula lie on the chest and back but are still appendicular. The sternum and ribs are axial, so do not mix them up.

notes.b: Most of the limb bones are long bones, and their structure shows how a bone can be both strong and light. Knowing the layers of a long bone also lets you label a section through one.
points: The limb bones named in the specification, except the patella, are long bones: a long shaft with a wider end at each joint. The patella is a small flat bone, so it is the exception.
The shaft is a hollow tube of dense compact bone. A tube is nearly as strong as a solid rod of the same width but much lighter, so the limb is strong but light enough to move quickly.
The wider ends are made of spongy bone, a lattice of thin bony struts that is light but strong along the lines of force, and that contains red bone marrow.
The central cavity of the shaft (the marrow cavity) contains yellow marrow.
The ends are covered with smooth articular cartilage (cartilage covering the joint surface) where they form joints. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.
Apart from the joint surfaces, the whole bone is covered by a tough membrane, the periosteum, to which tendons (which join muscle to bone) and ligaments (which join bone to bone) attach.

Diagram: a long bone (the femur) in longitudinal section, labelling compact bone, spongy bone, marrow cavity with yellow marrow, red marrow in the spongy bone, articular cartilage, periosteum and shaft.
notes.tip: If asked why long bones are hollow tubes, say a tube is nearly as strong as a solid rod of the same width but much lighter. You may also be asked to label a section of a long bone.

notes.b: The pectoral girdle is the shoulder girdle that hangs the arm from the trunk. Its design favours freedom of movement over strength, which is the opposite of the pelvic girdle.
points: The pectoral girdle is formed on each side by a clavicle and a scapula. It attaches the arm to the axial skeleton and is built for a wide range of movement rather than for bearing weight.
The clavicle (collarbone) is a slender, S-shaped bone running across the top of the chest from the sternum (breastbone) to the scapula.
The clavicle acts as a strut, holding the shoulder out to the side so the arm can swing freely, and passes forces from the arm to the axial skeleton.
Its joint with the sternum is the only bony connection between the arm and the axial skeleton, which is why the arm is so mobile.
The scapula (shoulder blade) is a large, flat, triangular bone lying on the back of the rib cage.
The scapula is not joined to the ribs or vertebrae but is held in place by muscles, so it can slide and rotate, increasing the range of movement of the arm.
Its large flat surface and ridges give a large area for attachment of shoulder and arm muscles, including the biceps and triceps. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.

The scapula has a shallow socket into which the rounded head of the humerus (the upper arm bone) fits, forming the shoulder joint, a ball-and-socket joint. The shallow socket allows the arm to move in almost every direction, including rotation, but makes the joint less stable than the hip.
notes.tip: Remember that the shoulder is more mobile and less stable than the hip. Do not reverse this when comparing them.

notes.b: The pelvic girdle is the hip girdle that joins the legs to the trunk. Because the legs carry the whole body, it is built for stability and strength rather than range of movement.
points: The pelvic girdle (pelvis) is a strong, bowl-shaped ring formed by the two hip bones, joined firmly to the sacrum (the base of the vertebral column) at the back and to each other at the front.
Each hip bone is made of several bones fused together; the names of these bones are not required.

The pelvic girdle is joined firmly to the vertebral column through the sacrum, so it is rigid. It carries the weight of the upper body and passes it to the legs, which makes it much stronger and less movable than the pectoral girdle.
It has a deep, cup-shaped socket on each side into which the head of the femur (the thigh bone) fits, forming the hip joint, a ball-and-socket joint.
The deep socket makes the hip very stable and suited to bearing weight, but it gives a smaller range of movement than the shoulder.
The pelvic girdle protects the organs of the lower abdomen: the bladder, lower intestine and reproductive organs, including the uterus.
Its broad surfaces anchor the large muscles of the legs and trunk.
The female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a larger, rounder central opening than the male pelvis, so that a baby's head can pass through during birth.
notes.tip: Do not list the names of the bones that make up each hip bone, as they are not required. Say only that each hip bone is several bones fused together.

notes.b: The two girdles do different jobs, and each difference in structure explains a difference in function. Set them side by side to answer comparison questions.
points: Attachment: the pectoral girdle is loosely attached to the axial skeleton by muscles, so the arm is free to move; the pelvic girdle is fused to the sacrum, so it is rigid.
Socket: the pectoral girdle has a shallow socket, which allows a wide range of movement; the pelvic girdle has a deep socket, which holds the femur firmly.
Function: the pectoral girdle gives mobility; the pelvic girdle gives stability and carries weight.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to compare the pectoral and pelvic girdles in structure and function. Give paired points on attachment, socket and function, and link each structure to its function.

notes.b: The arm has one bone in the upper arm and two in the forearm. Each joint between them is a different type, which gives the arm both stability and mobility.
points: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm. Its rounded head fits into the socket of the scapula at the shoulder, a ball-and-socket joint.

The lower end of the humerus meets the radius and ulna at the elbow, a hinge joint (a joint that bends in one direction only). Its long shaft gives attachment to the muscles that move the shoulder and elbow.
The ulna is the longer forearm bone, on the little-finger side.
The upper end of the ulna hooks around the end of the humerus, forming the main part of the elbow hinge and the point of the elbow, which stops the arm bending backwards beyond straight.
The triceps (the muscle at the back of the upper arm) is attached to the ulna. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.
The radius is the shorter forearm bone, on the thumb side. It forms most of the joint with the wrist.

At the elbow, the rounded head of the radius turns against the ulna in a pivot joint, so the radius can rotate around the ulna to turn the palm up or down. The biceps (the muscle at the front of the upper arm) is attached to the radius.
The two forearm bones make the hand both strong and highly mobile: the ulna gives a stable hinge at the elbow, and the radius allows rotation of the hand.
notes.tip: The radius is on the thumb side and the ulna on the little-finger side. Be ready to name and label the arm bones, and to state the function of a named bone.

notes.b: The leg has one bone in the thigh and two in the lower leg, plus the patella at the knee. These bones carry the body's weight and drive walking, running and jumping.
points: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
The rounded head of the femur fits into the deep socket of the pelvic girdle at the hip. Its lower end forms the knee joint, a hinge joint, with the tibia.
The thick shaft of compact bone carries the body's weight, and it gives attachment to the large thigh muscles used in walking, running and jumping.
The patella (kneecap) is a small, flat, roughly triangular bone at the front of the knee, embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps, the large muscle at the front of the thigh.
The patella protects the front of the knee joint and holds the tendon away from the joint, improving the leverage of the quadriceps when it straightens the leg.

The tibia (shinbone) is the larger, inner bone of the lower leg, on the big-toe side. It forms the knee joint with the femur and the ankle joint below, and carries almost all the weight passed down from the femur.

The fibula is the thin outer bone of the lower leg. It is not part of the knee joint and carries little weight, but it provides attachment for muscles of the lower leg and helps form and stabilise the outer side of the ankle.

The wrist, hand, ankle and foot bones are not named in the specification; label them on diagrams as wrist bones, hand bones, ankle bones and foot bones. Many small bones give the hands their fine, flexible movements and give the feet a flexible, weight-spreading base.
notes.tip: The patella is a limb bone in the appendicular skeleton, not part of the femur or tibia. The tibia is the larger inner bone and the fibula the thinner outer one, and the fibula is not part of the knee joint. Be ready to state the function of the patella, scapula or femur.

notes.b: The arm and the leg look different, but they follow the same basic plan. This similarity is a useful pattern to spot on a skeleton diagram.
points: The arm and the leg are built to the same plan: one bone in the upper part (humerus; femur), two in the lower part (radius and ulna; tibia and fibula), then many small bones in the wrist or ankle and five digits.

The same plan in the forelimbs of other vertebrates is evidence of common ancestry, because it suggests the animals inherited the pattern from a shared ancestor. There is more on this in Explaining biological phenomena.

notes.b: Putting the axial and appendicular parts together on one diagram shows how the girdles and limbs attach to the central skeleton.
points: Diagram: front view of the whole human skeleton, labelling the axial parts (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and the appendicular parts named in the specification (clavicle, scapula, pelvic girdle, humerus, radius, ulna, femur, patella, tibia and fibula), with the wrist, hand, ankle and foot bones labelled as groups.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name and label the bones of the arm, leg and pectoral girdle on a diagram of the skeleton. Label the wrist, hand, ankle and foot bones as groups only.

keyTerms.definition: The pectoral and pelvic girdles and the bones of the limbs attached to them.
The clavicle and scapula on each side, which attach the arm to the axial skeleton.
The strong, bowl-shaped ring of the two hip bones, fused to the sacrum, which carries the weight of the upper body to the legs.
The slender, S-shaped collarbone that acts as a strut holding the shoulder out to the side.
The large, flat shoulder blade, held by muscles, with a shallow socket for the head of the humerus.
The small, flat kneecap embedded in the quadriceps tendon at the front of the knee.
A bone with a long shaft and a wider end at each joint, with a hollow shaft of compact bone and spongy ends.
The tough membrane covering the whole bone, apart from the joint surfaces, to which tendons and ligaments attach.

questions.prompt: Name the two bones of the pectoral girdle and give one function of each.
questions.model: The two bones are the clavicle and the scapula. The clavicle (collarbone) acts as a strut, holding the shoulder out to the side so the arm can swing freely, and it passes forces from the arm to the axial skeleton. The scapula (shoulder blade) is held by muscles so that it can slide and rotate, increasing the range of movement of the arm; its shallow socket receives the head of the humerus and its large surface gives attachment to shoulder and arm muscles.

questions.prompt: Compare the structure of the pelvic girdle and the pectoral girdle and relate each to its function.
questions.model: The pectoral girdle is loosely attached to the axial skeleton by muscles, and its scapula has a shallow socket for the humerus. This allows a wide range of movement, which suits the arm's job of reaching and swinging, but the joint is less stable. The pelvic girdle is a rigid, bowl-shaped ring fused to the sacrum, and its deep socket holds the head of the femur. This makes the hip very stable and suited to bearing the body's weight and passing it to the legs, although it allows a smaller range of movement than the shoulder.

questions.prompt: Name the bones of the human leg and relate the structure of any two to their functions.
questions.model: The bones of the leg are the femur, patella, tibia and fibula. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body; its thick shaft of compact bone carries the body's weight and gives attachment to the large thigh muscles used in walking and running. The tibia is the larger, inner bone of the lower leg; it forms the knee and ankle joints and carries almost all the weight passed down from the femur. The fibula is thin and outer, takes little weight and is not part of the knee joint, but it gives attachment to lower leg muscles. The patella, embedded in the quadriceps tendon, protects the front of the knee and improves the leverage of the quadriceps.
